    Understanding badgers

    Goal¶

    Understand the building blocks — generators, selectors, DGPs, and pipelines — before going through the per-deficit tutorials.

    1. Where generators live: the module structure¶

    Generators are grouped first by modality (tabular_data, time_series, text, image, graph, geolocated_data), then by deficit family (outliers, noise, drift, missingness, imbalance). Every family is a Python package of modules, and every generator is a class whose name ends in Generator.

    2. Instantiate a generator¶

    A generator is a plain Python class. Each generator takes a numpy.random.Generator at construction:

    gen = SomeGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(seed))
    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    # Setup: imports and a small example dataset used throughout the notebook
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
import scipy.stats

from numpy.random import default_rng
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

X, cls = make_blobs(n_samples=100, centers=3, cluster_std=0.5, random_state=0)

plt.figure(figsize=(4, 3))
plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=cls, cmap="tab10", s=15)
plt.title("Example dataset X (100 rows, 2 columns)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    # Setup: imports and a small example dataset used throughout the notebook import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import networkx as nx import scipy.stats from numpy.random import default_rng from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs X, cls = make_blobs(n_samples=100, centers=3, cluster_std=0.5, random_state=0) plt.figure(figsize=(4, 3)) plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=cls, cmap="tab10", s=15) plt.title("Example dataset X (100 rows, 2 columns)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Adding rows, exemplified: outliers¶

    This example adds 10 outliers to X. Note what happens to the shape: the outliers are appended as new rows, so Xt is bigger than X.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,
)

gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0))

Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(),
                  selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=10, rng=default_rng(0)),
                  out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")
print('outliers:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)
    from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import ( OutlierSamplingGenerator, ) gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0)) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=10, rng=default_rng(0)), out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore") print('outliers:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)

    Deficit labels¶

    Some generators save which rows have been modified and expose this information through a dedicated getter — for outliers, get_outliers_labels():

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    labels = gen.get_outliers_labels()      # bool array: True = outlier row
print('labels:', labels.dtype, 'length', len(labels), '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum()))
print('first rows are original:', not labels[:len(X)].any())
print('last rows are outliers:', labels[len(X):].all())
    labels = gen.get_outliers_labels() # bool array: True = outlier row print('labels:', labels.dtype, 'length', len(labels), '| outlier rows:', int(labels.sum())) print('first rows are original:', not labels[:len(X)].any()) print('last rows are outliers:', labels[len(X):].all())

axes[0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=cls, cmap="tab10", s=15)
axes[0].set_title(f"Original X {X.shape}")

    4. Shape rules: what happens to Xt¶

    The shape of Xt depends on the deficit family — there are exactly three modes:

    Mode Effect on shape
    Adding rows Xt is larger than X (deficit rows appended)
    Changing values Xt has the same shape as X (existing values are changed)
    Removing rows Xt is smaller than X (affected rows are dropped)

    Changing values, exemplified: noise¶

    Additive noise replaces the existing values in place, so 100 rows stay 100 rows:

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator

gen = AdditiveNoiseGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0))
Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), distribution=scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5))
print('noise (values changed, same shape):', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator gen = AdditiveNoiseGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0)) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), distribution=scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5)) print('noise (values changed, same shape):', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape) 
    noise (values changed, same shape): (100, 2) -> (100, 2)

    Removing rows, exemplified: imbalance¶

    An imbalance generator removes the rows affected by the deficit. The only thing it needs to know is which rows — that decision is packaged in a selector (a boolean mask per column). Selectors are their own concept and get a full section below (section 5); here we just use one preset so the shape rule is visible: about half of the 100 rows are removed.

    In [ ]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.imbalance import UndersamplingGenerator
from badgers.core.selectors import BernoulliSelector

gen = UndersamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(1))
selector = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.5, rng=default_rng(2))

Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=selector)
print('imbalance (rows removed):', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)
    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.imbalance import UndersamplingGenerator from badgers.core.selectors import BernoulliSelector gen = UndersamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(1)) selector = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.5, rng=default_rng(2)) Xt = gen.generate(X.copy(), selector=selector) print('imbalance (rows removed):', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)
    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    # Visualize: rows removed — the rows marked True by the selector are dropped
mask = selector(X)[0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
axes[0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=np.where(mask, "C3", "C0"), s=15)
axes[0].set_title(f"Original X {X.shape}\n(red = selector True)")
axes[1].scatter(Xt[:, 0], Xt[:, 1], s=15, c="C0")
axes[1].set_title(f"Xt {Xt.shape}\n(selected rows removed)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    5. Selectors: which rows get the deficit¶

    Generators (drift, missingness, noise, imbalance, ...) accept a selector: an object that decides which rows receive the deficit.

    The contract¶

    Selectors are index-only: they work on column positions, never on variable names (no column_mapping in the selector layer).

    values = selector(X)   # -> dict[int, spec]

    The dict keys are the column positions the deficit applies to. Per target column the spec is either:

    • a boolean mask — True = the deficit is applied to that row (deterministic), or
    • a float in [0, 1] (scalar = one level for the whole column) or a (n,) array — the probability that the deficit is applied to that row (1.0 = definitely, 0.0 = never).

    The presets are self-contained: the positions they cover (columns) and the positions they read (class_column, column, driver) are all bound at construction as bare ints. Causal generators pass their targets positionally: the selector's columns ARE the intervention targets.

    The presets¶

    Badgers ships selectors (see badgers.core.selectors):

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.core.selectors import BernoulliSelector, TopQuantileSelector

X_raw, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=2, random_state=3)

# BernoulliSelector realizes its rng at call time and returns a
# boolean mask (True = affected row).
selector = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.2, rng=default_rng(0))
mask = selector(X_raw)[0]
print('BernoulliSelector mask dtype:', mask.dtype, '| affected rows:', int(mask.sum()))

# A deterministic rule: rows in the top 10% of f0.
selector = TopQuantileSelector([0], column=0, quantile=0.9)
mask = selector(X_raw)[0]
print('TopQuantileSelector mask dtype:', mask.dtype, '| affected rows:', int(mask.sum()))

# Visualize both masks side by side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
mask_b = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.2, rng=default_rng(0))(X_raw)[0]
mask_q = TopQuantileSelector([0], column=0, quantile=0.9)(X_raw)[0]
axes[0].scatter(X_raw[:, 0], X_raw[:, 1], c=np.where(mask_b, "C3", "C0"), s=15)
axes[0].set_title("BernoulliSelector rate=0.2\n(red = affected)")
axes[1].scatter(X_raw[:, 0], X_raw[:, 1], c=np.where(mask_q, "C3", "C0"), s=15)
axes[1].set_title("TopQuantileSelector quantile=0.9\n(red = affected)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    from badgers.core.selectors import BernoulliSelector, TopQuantileSelector X_raw, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=2, random_state=3) # BernoulliSelector realizes its rng at call time and returns a # boolean mask (True = affected row). selector = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.2, rng=default_rng(0)) mask = selector(X_raw)[0] print('BernoulliSelector mask dtype:', mask.dtype, '| affected rows:', int(mask.sum())) # A deterministic rule: rows in the top 10% of f0. selector = TopQuantileSelector([0], column=0, quantile=0.9) mask = selector(X_raw)[0] print('TopQuantileSelector mask dtype:', mask.dtype, '| affected rows:', int(mask.sum())) # Visualize both masks side by side fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5), sharex=True, sharey=True) mask_b = BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.2, rng=default_rng(0))(X_raw)[0] mask_q = TopQuantileSelector([0], column=0, quantile=0.9)(X_raw)[0] axes[0].scatter(X_raw[:, 0], X_raw[:, 1], c=np.where(mask_b, "C3", "C0"), s=15) axes[0].set_title("BernoulliSelector rate=0.2\n(red = affected)") axes[1].scatter(X_raw[:, 0], X_raw[:, 1], c=np.where(mask_q, "C3", "C0"), s=15) axes[1].set_title("TopQuantileSelector quantile=0.9\n(red = affected)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show()

    6. Data-generating processes (DGP) and structural causal models (SCM)¶

    Some generators use a structural causal model (SCM) to represent the underlying data-generating process (DGP). An SCM encodes how the columns come about, not just what they look like: each column is generated from its causal parents plus noise, following the edges of a causal graph. In badgers a DGP is an object that bundles:

    • a networkx.DiGraph describing the causal structure (an edge A -> B means A is a cause of B),
    • a column_mapping from node names to column positions in X, and
    • per-node causal mechanisms estimated from the data (e.g., a linear regression of the child on its parents plus a noise term).

    This is what makes causal generators different from plain value edits: they intervene on a node (fix its values, do(B = v)), then sample — i.e. recompute that node's children and all their descendants from the SCM, so the whole downstream part of the data stays consistent with the causal structure.

    Functions:¶

    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm).fit(X)                  # fit mechanisms (scm: a dowhy-gcm StructuralCausalModel)
Xs = dgp.sample(rng, n)                      # sample fresh data from the SCM
Xi = dgp.intervene(X.copy(), ['B'], [values], rng=rng)  # do(B = ...), descendants recomputed

    Backends:¶

    The shipped backends are two SCM adapters in badgers.core.dgp.backends: GcmSCMDGP wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel (extra badgers[dowhy]) and PyMCSCMDGP wraps a PyMC pm.Model (extra badgers[pymc]) — build the SCM with the wrapped library's own API, then hand it over. There is no default backend: causal generators require an explicit dgp=. See the dev notebook Using DGPs for the two adapters in action.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    import networkx as nx
import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP

# DGP definition (linear model with additive noise):
# X_0 = Normal distribution mu=0, sigma=1
# X_1 = 2 * X_0 + noise
# X_2 = 0.5 * X_1 + noise

graph = nx.DiGraph([('A', 'B'), ('B', 'C')])
column_mapping = {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 2}

rng = default_rng(0)
X_raw = np.zeros((500, 3))
X_raw[:, 0] = rng.normal(size=500)
X_raw[:, 1] = 2.0 * X_raw[:, 0] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500)
X_raw[:, 2] = 0.5 * X_raw[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500)

scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
for node in graph.nodes:
    if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
        scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
    else:
        scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
            prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))

dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm, column_mapping).fit(X_raw)

# sample fresh data from the fitted DGP (signature: sample(rng, n))
Xs = dgp.sample(default_rng(1), 10)
print('sampled shape:', Xs.shape)

# intervene in place: pass a copy, fix the values in B (all = 10), recompute C downstream
Xi = dgp.intervene(X_raw.copy(), ['B'], [np.full(500, 10.0)], rng=default_rng(2))
print('B pinned:', np.allclose(Xi[:, 1], 10.0))
print('C propagated (B=10 -> C~5):', np.allclose(Xi[:, 2], 5.0, atol=0.5))
    import networkx as nx import dowhy.gcm as gcm from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP # DGP definition (linear model with additive noise): # X_0 = Normal distribution mu=0, sigma=1 # X_1 = 2 * X_0 + noise # X_2 = 0.5 * X_1 + noise graph = nx.DiGraph([('A', 'B'), ('B', 'C')]) column_mapping = {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 2} rng = default_rng(0) X_raw = np.zeros((500, 3)) X_raw[:, 0] = rng.normal(size=500) X_raw[:, 1] = 2.0 * X_raw[:, 0] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500) X_raw[:, 2] = 0.5 * X_raw[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500) scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph) for node in graph.nodes: if not list(graph.predecessors(node)): scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution()) else: scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel( prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor())) dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm, column_mapping).fit(X_raw) # sample fresh data from the fitted DGP (signature: sample(rng, n)) Xs = dgp.sample(default_rng(1), 10) print('sampled shape:', Xs.shape) # intervene in place: pass a copy, fix the values in B (all = 10), recompute C downstream Xi = dgp.intervene(X_raw.copy(), ['B'], [np.full(500, 10.0)], rng=default_rng(2)) print('B pinned:', np.allclose(Xi[:, 1], 10.0)) print('C propagated (B=10 -> C~5):', np.allclose(Xi[:, 2], 5.0, atol=0.5))

    7. Pipelines: chaining deficits¶
    Deficits compose. A Pipeline takes a dict of generators (the keys
are step names) and applies them in order, passing each output to the
next step. Per-step parameters are passed at generate() time keyed
by the step name:
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [ ]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    from badgers.core.pipeline import Pipeline
from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise import AdditiveNoiseGenerator
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,
)

pipeline = Pipeline({
    "noise": AdditiveNoiseGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(3)),
    "outliers": OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(4)),
})
Xt = pipeline.generate(X.copy(), params={
    "noise": {"distribution": scipy.stats.norm(scale=0.5)},
    "outliers": {
        "selector": CountSelector([0, 1], count=10, rng=default_rng(4)),
        "out_of_distribution_sampler": "hypersphere",
    },
})
print('pipeline output:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)

    8. Randomness¶
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Badgers generators never touch global random state. The sequence of random numbers they use is the one supplied at construction, so:
    

      

    • same seed => identical outputs, bit for bit;
      • 

    • the stream is owned by the caller — create one generator and pass
it to several generators to keep a single reproducible stream.
      • 

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [ ]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    from numpy.random import default_rng
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,
)

gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0))
print(gen)

from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,

gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(0))
print(gen)
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Same seed, same output¶
    Two generators built from the same seed
produce bit-identical results — the reproducibility contract in action:
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [ ]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,
)

X_ex, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=100, centers=2, random_state=2)   # known-good data


def make_outliers(seed):
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(seed))
    return gen.generate(X_ex,
                        selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=10, rng=default_rng(seed)),
                        out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")


Xt1 = make_outliers(42)
Xt2 = make_outliers(42)
print('same seed -> identical output:', np.array_equal(Xt1, Xt2))

Xt3 = make_outliers(7)
print('different seed -> different output:', not np.array_equal(Xt1, Xt3))

    

    import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

from badgers.core.selectors import CountSelector
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.outliers.sampling import (
    OutlierSamplingGenerator,
)

X_ex, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=100, centers=2, random_state=2)   # known-good data


def make_outliers(seed):
    gen = OutlierSamplingGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(seed))
    return gen.generate(X_ex,
                        selector=CountSelector([0, 1], count=10, rng=default_rng(seed)),
                        out_of_distribution_sampler="zscore")


Xt1 = make_outliers(42)
Xt2 = make_outliers(42)
print('same seed -> identical output:', np.array_equal(Xt1, Xt2))

Xt3 = make_outliers(7)
print('different seed -> different output:', not np.array_equal(Xt1, Xt3))

    Takeaways¶
      

    • Generators are instantiated with an rng and called via generate(X, **params) — they take X only and return the single generated object Xt; target-like data lives in dedicated columns of X.
      • 

    • Shape rules: appending (outliers), shape-preserving (noise, missingness), row-changing (imbalance: removing or duplicating rows).
      • 

    • Selectors decide which rows are affected; DGPs model the data-generating process; pipelines compose generators.
      •
